title: Cache
summary: Keep the answers you keep needing somewhere faster and closer. The hard part is not storing them — it is knowing when they have gone stale.
analogy: Keeping the three books you are actually using on your desk instead of walking to the library each time. The desk is small, so you keep only what you reach for most; and if the library issues a corrected edition, the copy on your desk is quietly wrong until you notice.

explanation.beginner: Fetching data from a database takes a few milliseconds; fetching it from memory takes microseconds. If the same data is requested over and over, storing it in a fast in-memory store like Redis means most requests never touch the database at all. The catch is that when the underlying data changes, the cached copy is out of date — so every cache needs a rule for when entries expire or get removed.
explanation.interview: An in-memory tier exploiting temporal and spatial locality. Effectiveness is governed by the hit rate: effective latency = hit_rate × cache_latency + (1 - hit_rate) × origin_latency, so 95% hits removes about 95% of origin load. The real design decisions are the write policy (cache-aside, write-through, write-behind), the invalidation strategy (TTL, explicit, versioned keys) and the eviction policy (LRU, LFU, TTL). Failure modes worth naming: stampede on expiry, cache penetration by missing keys, and inconsistency windows after writes.

nodes.label: Cache (Redis)
nodes.note: Sub-millisecond in-memory lookups. Volatile by design: losing it must be survivable.

without: Database CPU saturates; p99 latency climbs; connection pools exhaust
with: At a 95% hit rate, 1,000 reads/s => ~50 database queries/s
Reads served in ~0.5 ms instead of ~5 ms
why.conclusion: Lower latency, 20x less database load, and headroom you did not have to buy.

nodes.label: Database
nodes.note: The source of truth. Only cache misses reach it.

without: Every read hits the database, whose capacity is the hardest and most expensive thing to grow
Read latency is bounded by disk and network
Traffic spikes translate directly into database load
with: Origin load drops by roughly the hit rate
Spikes are absorbed by the cheap tier
why.conclusion: Caching is the highest-leverage performance change in most systems — and the most common source of 'why is this data wrong?'.

whenToUse: The same data is requested repeatedly
Slightly stale data is acceptable — and you can say how stale
whenNotToUse: Data must be exactly current (account balances at the moment of a transfer)
Every key is read roughly once — you pay the write cost and never get a hit
The working set is so large that the hit rate would be low anyway
Write-heavy workloads, where invalidation costs more than it saves

pros: Cache failure degrades to slow, not broken
Simple and by far the most common
cons: First request per key is always a miss
Stale data possible between write and invalidation
Vulnerable to stampede when a hot key expires

pros: Cache is always consistent with the database
cons: Caches data that may never be read
Data loss if the cache dies before flushing — unacceptable for anything that matters

pros: Dead simple, self-healing, no invalidation bugs

quiz.question: At a 95% cache hit rate with cache reads at 0.5 ms and database reads at 5 ms, what is the average read latency?
quiz.explanation: 0.95 × 0.5 + 0.05 × 5 = 0.475 + 0.25 = 0.725 ms. Note how much the 5% of misses still contribute — which is why tail latency stays dominated by the origin.

quiz.question: A popular cached key expires and 10,000 concurrent requests all miss and hit the database at once. What is this called and how do you prevent it?
options: Cache penetration; use a bloom filter
Cache stampede; use a mutex/single-flight so one request refills while others wait, plus randomised TTL jitter
quiz.explanation: A stampede (or thundering herd). Standard fixes: single-flight locking per key, staggered TTLs, and proactive refresh shortly before expiry.

quiz.question: Which data is the worst candidate for caching?
options: A user's current account balance during a transfer
quiz.explanation: Stale money is a correctness bug, not a performance trade-off. Cache things where a small staleness window is acceptable and say explicitly how large that window is.
